1.g3 d5 2.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop bears on d5 and along the long diagonal towards b7, and White can castle quickly once the knight is out. It controls the centre from a distance instead of occupying it, which keeps White flexible but leaves Black free to take the centre first, so White has to challenge it later.

1.g3 d5 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square, where it covers d4 and e5, so that 2...e5? loses a pawn to 3.Nxe5. With the bishop on g2 and quick castling to follow, White builds a flexible set-up, but Black still holds the larger share of the centre and White has to undermine it later.

1.g3 d5 2.d4.strategy: Claims the centre at once, with g3 already played and the bishop to come to g2. It is sound but slow: d5 is not yet challenged, so Black can develop comfortably.

1.g3 d5 2.c4.strategy: Attacks d5 from the flank, before the bishop on g2 can add pressure along the long diagonal. After 2...dxc4 White regains the pawn with Qa4+ and Qxc4, while Black can also push the d-pawn and gain space. It is sound but rarely played.

1.g3 d5 2.d3.strategy: Supports a later e4 and keeps the pieces flexible, heading for a King's Indian Attack set-up. It is sound but passive: Black takes the centre and meets e4 on equal terms.

1.g3 d5 2.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2 so that both bishops bear on the long diagonals in a double fianchetto, with the kingside development to follow. It is sound but slow: Black can take space in the centre while White has nothing against d5 yet.

1.g3 d5 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece, eyes d5 and prepares e4, but blocks the c-pawn and invites 2...d4. The knight must then move again and is challenged on its new square, so Black gains space with a tempo.

1.g3 d5 2.f4.strategy: Controls e5 and heads for a set-up with the knight on f3, the bishop on g2 and quick castling. It is sound, but it loosens the a7–g1 diagonal and the e3 square, and Black develops comfortably.

1.g3 d5 2.a3.strategy: Spends a tempo on a flank move that prepares only a later b4. Nothing in the centre or in White's development improves, and Black occupies the centre unhindered.

1.g3 d5 2.a4.strategy: Gains queenside space but contributes nothing to the centre or to development, and the a-pawn can no longer support a later b4. Black builds freely and White is a tempo behind.

1.g3 d5 2.b4.strategy: Grabs queenside space and prepares Bb2, but the pawn on b4 lacks support: ...a5 attacks it at once, and once the e-pawn moves the f8 bishop hits it too. Black develops freely while White has to look after the pawn.

1.g3 d5 2.c3.strategy: Supports a later d4, but takes c3 from the b1 knight, which has to develop via d2 or a3, and does nothing yet against d5. Black develops freely.

1.g3 d5 2.e3.strategy: Opens a diagonal for the f1 bishop, which already had g2, and shuts in the c1 bishop. The pawn covers d4 but does nothing against d5, so Black can take space or simply develop.

1.g3 d5 2.f3.strategy: Prepares e4 but takes f3 from the king's knight and opens the a7–g1 diagonal, which makes short castling less safe. Black builds the centre while White's development is awkward.

1.g3 d5 2.h3.strategy: Stops ...Bg4 but is a slow move that neither develops a piece nor contests the centre. Black occupies the centre and has the easier game.

1.g3 d5 2.h4.strategy: Starts a kingside pawn advance with h5 in mind, but there is nothing to attack yet: the move ignores the centre and weakens the g3 pawn's support. Black can answer in kind or simply build in the centre.

1.g3 d5 2.Na3.strategy: Heads for b5, but ...c6 takes that square away and the d5 pawn already controls c4, so the knight has few useful squares. It leaves b1 for the rim, blocks the a-pawn and does nothing for the centre.

1.g3 d5 2.Bh3.strategy: Offers a bishop trade after 2...Bxh3 3.Nxh3, which gives up the fianchetto, puts the knight on the rim and leaves the long diagonal and the light squares weak. Black can also ignore it and build the centre.

1.g3 d5 2.Nh3.strategy: Keeps g2 free for the bishop and heads for f4 to press on d5, but 2...e5 covers f4 and leaves the knight on the rim with no good square to go to. Black develops freely while White still has to bring the knight back into play.

1.g3 d5 2.e4.strategy: Gambits the e-pawn on the strength of the fianchetto, but after 2...dxe4 3.Bg2 Black holds the extra pawn. White's lead in development is too small to pay for it.

1.g3 d5 2.g4.strategy: Hangs the pawn: 2...Bxg4 wins it, because the queen is blocked by the e2 pawn and nothing defends g4. White has no lead in development in return, and 3.h3 only chases the bishop to a good square.

1.g3 d5.background: The most frequent reply to 1.g3: in each of the five game databases compared in Wikibooks' opening theory, 1...d5 is played in roughly 28 to 37 percent of the games.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 Nf6.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight guards d5 and eyes e4 while committing Black to nothing else. Every set-up stays open, so White decides whether the game becomes a slow build-up or a fight for the centre with c4.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 c6.name: Hungarian Opening: Slav Formation
1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 c6.background: The name refers to the Slav Defence, 1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6, which has the same pawns on c6 and d5. That opening was analysed as early as 1590 but explored extensively only from the 1920s, and many masters of Slavic descent, among them Alapin, Alekhine, Bogoljubov and Vidmar, helped develop its theory.
1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 c6.strategy: Supports d5 with a second pawn, which blunts the g2 bishop on the long diagonal and takes the sting out of c4. The cost is the c6 square: the b8 knight has to develop via d7, and the c8 bishop should come out before ...e6 closes the chain. A solid structure in which White can build slowly or press with c4.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 c5.name: Hungarian Opening: Reversed Modern Defence
1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 c5.strategy: Takes control of d4 and gains queenside space, aiming at active play against White's centre. The cost is d5, which only the queen guards against the g2 bishop, so c4 puts it under real pressure. More ambitious than ...c6, but less solid.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 e5.strategy: Takes the centre with a second pawn. Both central pawns need support: the g2 bishop and c4 aim at d5, while a knight and the d-pawn hit e5. Black claims space at once, and White has to decide whether to challenge the centre or build quietly.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 e6.name: Hungarian Opening: Catalan Formation
1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 e6.background: The name refers to the Catalan Opening, in which White plays d4 and c4 and fianchettoes the bishop on g2. That opening takes its name from Catalonia: the organisers of the 1929 Barcelona tournament asked Savielly Tartakower to create a new variation in homage to Catalonia's chess history.
1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 e6.strategy: Supports d5 and opens the f8 bishop's diagonal, preparing quick development and castling. Sound but passive: the c8 bishop stays shut in behind e6, and White can pressure d5 or build at leisure.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight towards d4 and e5, but blocks the c-pawn, so ...c6 can no longer support d5. After c4 the d5 pawn is attacked twice and guarded only by the queen. Playable, but developing the other knight does not block the c-pawn.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 f5.strategy: Takes e4 from White and aims for a solid wall of pawns on c6, d5, e6 and f5. It is sturdy, but it leaves a hole on e5 that a White knight can use, loosens the e8–h5 diagonal and shuts in the c8 bishop once the e-pawn reaches e6.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 g6.strategy: Mirrors White's set-up with a fianchettoed bishop and quick castling. The g7 bishop does nothing for d5, so c4 tests the pawn at once: it is attacked twice and guarded only by the queen. Sound, but less flexible than developing the knight.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 d4.strategy: Gains space and takes c3 and e3 from White's pieces, though the advanced pawn needs support. The cost is the long diagonal: with d5 vacated the g2 bishop bears on b7, so the c8 bishop is tied to its defence until a pawn or knight on c6 closes the line, and White can undermine the advanced pawn later.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 Be6.strategy: Guards d5 but blocks the e7 pawn, so the f8 bishop can come out only via ...g6, and with the c8 bishop gone b7 has no guard against c4 and Qb3. White also gains time by bringing a knight to g5, hitting the bishop.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 Bf5.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain but takes the guard away from b7. After 3.c4 c6 4.cxd5 cxd5 5.Qb3 the queen hits b7 and, together with the g2 bishop, d5, so Black has to defend both pawns at once.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 Bg4.strategy: Develops the bishop before White's knight is on f3, so it pins nothing, and h3 makes it move again at once. With the bishop gone from c8, b7 has no guard, and c4 with Qb3 hits b7 and d5 together.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 Qd7.strategy: Keeps d5 guarded, but the queen blocks the c8 bishop and takes d7 from the b8 knight, so Black's development stalls and the queen usually has to move again.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 Qd6.strategy: Brings the queen out before any minor piece. 3.Nc3 attacks d5 a second time and threatens Nb5 against the queen and c7, so Black loses time defending while White prepares e4.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it guards neither d5 nor e5 and needs another move, to b4 or c7, to help hold d5. White builds with c4 and Nf3 unhindered.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 Nh6.strategy: Heads for f5 instead of f6, the natural square from which the knight guards d5 and covers e4. Once White's d-pawn has moved, Bxh6 gxh6 doubles Black's h-pawns.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 a6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a flank move that prepares only ...b5. Nothing is done for the centre or for development, and White can take space with c4 or d4 and develop freely.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 a5.strategy: Gains queenside space and stops b4, but does nothing for the centre or development. White continues developing undisturbed.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, but the d5 pawn blocks that bishop, and with the b-pawn gone the long diagonal opens towards a8 as soon as d5 moves: after 3.c4 dxc4? 4.Bxa8 White wins at least the exchange.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 b5.strategy: Advances a flank pawn before developing. 3.Nc3 attacks b5 and d5 together, so Black has to answer ...c6, and the pawns on b5, c6 and d5 leave a lasting hole on c5.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 f6.strategy: Prepares ...e5, but takes the best square from the g8 knight, weakens the e8-h5 diagonal and the e6 square, and develops nothing. White takes the centre with c4 or d4.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 g5.strategy: Weakens f5, h5 and the a1–h8 diagonal without developing anything, and 3.h4 attacks the unprotected pawn at once. The kingside is loosened for good, and the king has no safe home there.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 h6.strategy: Takes g5 from White's pieces, but White has not threatened to go there, and nothing is done for development or the centre. The tempo is better spent on a developing move.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 h5.strategy: Prepares ...h4 against g3, but with no piece developed the attack is premature. It loosens g5 and the kingside and gives White time to take the centre with c4 or d4.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 Nd7.strategy: Blocks the queen's protection of d5, so 3.Bxd5 wins a pawn; ...Nb6 only gains a tempo against the bishop, which retreats with the pawn won.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 Bd7.strategy: Blocks the queen's protection of d5 and leaves b7 without its bishop, so 3.Bxd5 wins a pawn and attacks b7 as well.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 Kd7.strategy: Blocks the d-file, so d5 loses the queen's protection and 3.Bxd5 wins a pawn; the king also gives up castling and stands in the centre.

1.g3 d5 2.Bg2 Bh3.strategy: Attacks the g2 bishop but hangs its own: 3.Bxh3 or 3.Nxh3 wins a whole piece, since nothing protects h3.

1.g3 d5 2.Nh3 e5.strategy: Puts a second pawn in the centre and takes d4 and f4 away from White's pieces. The knight on the rim has no active role, so Black's space is the lasting feature of the opening, and White must show that the fianchetto set-up can undermine it.
